newsitem.title: UK: Brent cash market thin, wet market still pressured.
newsitem.headline: Brent cash market thin, wet market still pressured.

text.p: The North Sea physical and cash markets were thinly talked on Tuesday, with buyers sticking to the sidelines in anticipation of further falls, traders said.

Unsold wet Brent and other North Sea grades were trapped in the region by a narrow transatlantic arbitrage. The premium for July Brent over July NYMEX crude has slipped to just $1.00, 50 cents off the differential North Sea sellers generally require for profitable transatlantic sales.
Dated Brent slipped some 13 cents on Monday to trade at July Brent -62 cents. A trading house which kept two cargoes from the paper chains on Monday was expected to reoffer them.
One Brent cargo, deferred from June 14-16 to 25-27 was due to turn wet on Tuesday.
Other North Sea grades have also slipped, with June barrels still abundant.
A Statfjord traded at just Dated Brent plus one cent, three cents off a deal on Friday, and 24 cents down on a deal earlier last week.
Other trades were heard to have been conducted on a private and confidential basis.
"In this difficult market everything is p+c," said one Norwegian producer.
Those sellers with storage were building stocks, traders said.
"Buyers are very relaxed at the moment and they won't come in while the see the market falling," said one.
The Brent paper market was quiet, with no CFDs or intermonth spreads heard traded.
CFDs for next week (June 16-20) were valued around August Brent -68 cents, and the next week (June 23-27) at August -60 cents.
The June/July intermonth spread was offered at -35 cents, but bids were much lower.
July/August held at the level traded in the U.S. aftermarket at around -30/-28 cents.
Outright July paper recovered slightly from Monday's losses, trading at $17.78 and $17.73 a barrel. The July Brent contract was 19 cents up at $17.75 on the IPE screen at 1150 GMT.
In the Mediterranean, one trader reported a Urals done on Friday at a firmer $1.18 discount to benchmark Dated Brent but others said the value looked too high.
"I doubt that. I just don't see it. I mean it's possible but there are other cargoes available," one said. "I'd put the market closer to the upper 20s."
Traders said available Urals cargoes comprised at least two one million barrel stems including a 19-20 loader and a 23-24 loader and two 80,000 tonners including a 22-23 loader and a 26-27 loader.

"What is clear is that this is a favourable moment to sell," said one trader. "There has been a lot of noise about this -$1.18 deal and we all know the Iraqis are coming up again - there is even talk that someone is already looking for a (June) 21-22 loader for a Kirkuk."
"And the closer we get to the end of June the closer we get to the July Russian programmes.
"Although people say they don't expect Kirkuk until July, this is just speculation at the end of the day. The truth is still out there waiting to be discovered, just like the X-Files."
In West Africans, Qua Iboe continued to be assessed unchanged at a premium in the mid-30s over Dated Brent, with Bonny Light in the low to mid-40s.

One Asian trader was heard picking up an Odudu at a discount of around five cents to Dated on Monday and traders also reported talk that two Osos loading in the second and third decade had changed hands but there were no immediate details.
--Rosalind Russell, Bill Maclean, London Newsroom +44 171 542
